Peter Breaks Through
A skeleton leaf from the window
The night nursery at 14, in London
Mrs Darling is sewing by the night-nursery fire. Speak with her.
Mrs Darling: "All children, except one, grow up." She is tidying up her children's minds, as every good mother does after they are asleep.
Nana, the nurse, is by her kennel. (She is a Newfoundland dog, and a treasure.)
Nana wags, once, properly. She has the bath ready and the medicine counted. She had a genius for knowing when a cough is a thing to have no patience with.
A skeleton leaf: not from any tree in England.
There are strange leaves on the floor by the window. Pick them up.
"Skeleton leaves," Mrs Darling murmurs, "very strange leaves." They were very strange leaves, and she was sure they did not come from any tree in England.
show her the leaves
Show the leaves to Mrs Darling.
In her children's minds, among the maps of the Neverland, she had found a name she did not know: Peter. "He is rather cocky," Wendy had said. Mrs Darling dozes off by the fire.
Wait by the window and watch. Something is out there in the night.
The window blew open, and a boy dropped on the floor: clad in skeleton leaves, with all his first teeth. Mrs Darling screamed.
Nana sprang at the boy! See what she has got.
He leapt lightly through the window. Nana slammed it down, too late to catch him, but his shadow had not had time to get out: slam went the window and snapped it off.
His shadow lies on the floor under the window. Pick it up.
It was quite the ordinary kind. Mrs Darling rolled it up carefully.
The top drawer of the chest
put the shadow away
Put the shadow in the top drawer of the chest, until a good time comes to tell Mr Darling.
Into the drawer it went. It was a Friday. Of course it was a Friday.
Mr Darling's white tie
The evening of the party at 27
Mr Darling is dressing for the party and cannot tie his tie. Help him.

"This tie, it will not tie. Not round my neck! Round the bed-post, oh yes; twenty times have I made it up round the bed-post." You tie it at last, and he is all good humour, and dances Michael round the room.
Ask Mrs Darling about the boy and the shadow.
She tells him all about it. "It is nobody I know," says Mr Darling, examining the shadow, "but he does look a scoundrel."
It is medicine time, and Michael will not take his.
"Won't! Won't!" "Be a man, Michael." "Father, you take yours first." Mr Darling's medicine is much nastier.
Mr Darling's medicine, hidden on top of the wardrobe
Mr Darling's own medicine is missing. (He hid it on top of the wardrobe, in case.) Fetch it.
"I thought I had lost it," he says, not very glad. Michael takes his like a man. Father does not.
watch what happens
Mr Darling has a 'splendid joke'. Watch at Nana's bowl.
He poured his medicine into Nana's bowl. Nana lapped it, then gave him such a look; not an angry look; and crept into her kennel. Nobody laughed.
"I won't have that dog lording it in my nursery!" He drags Nana down to the yard to chain her. Follow them (the door to the landing, and down).
There he tied her up. It was not true that he was a strong man; he simply had too strong a need for admiration.
She is not barking out of temper. She is barking because she smells danger. Wendy knew. "That is not her unhappy bark. That is her bark when she smells danger."
Go back up to the nursery.
Mrs Darling tucks the children up in their beds.
The little flame comes up, steady.
Light the three night-lights by the beds.
"Dear night-lights that protect my sleeping babes, burn clear and steadfast tonight."
The Darlings are going out to dinner at 27. Say good night.
They went out under the stars. The stars were watching. A little star in the Milky Way screamed out: "Now, Peter!"
Come Away, Come Away!
Wendy's thimble (a 'kiss')
That same night, with the Darlings out
Keep still in the dark, and watch the night-lights.
Mrs Darling's night-light blinked and yawned and went out; the other two did too. And there was another light in the room now, a thousand times brighter, looking for Peter's shadow.
The jug on the washstand
The darting light has hidden. Look in the jug.
Tinker Bell! No longer than your hand, exquisitely gowned in a skeleton leaf, cut low and square. She was a common fairy, who mended the pots and kettles.
A boy has come in at the window. Who is he?
"Tinker Bell," he called softly, "Tink, where are you? Do you know where they put my shadow?" It is Peter Pan.
Show Peter where his shadow is: the top drawer of the chest.
He scattered the contents of the drawers with both hands, found his shadow, and in his delight shut Tinker Bell up in the drawer.
watch Peter try it
Peter is trying to stick his shadow on with soap.
It would not stick. A shudder went through him, and he sat on the floor and cried.
His crying wakes Wendy.
"Boy, why are you crying?" "What's your name?" "Wendy Moira Angela Darling. What is yours?" "Peter Pan." "It must be sewn on," she said, just a little patronisingly.
Wendy sews; it hurts, but he bears it.
Help Wendy sew the shadow on (her housewife is on the chair).
The shadow was on, a little creased. Peter jumped about in the wildest glee. "Oh, the cleverness of me!"
hold out your hand
Peter wants to give Wendy a kiss. (He does not know what one is.)
He dropped an acorn button into her hand: his kiss. She gave him her thimble: hers. He thought it was a kiss, and she put the button on a chain round her neck.
Hear what Peter tells Wendy about the Neverland.
The Lost Boys, the children who fall out of their perambulators; the mermaids; and stories. "Wendy, come with me and tell the other boys. You could tuck us in at night."
Wake John and Michael.
"Can you really fly?" Peter flew round the room, taking the mantelpiece on the way. "How topping!"
Peter blows fairy dust on you. Think lovely wonderful thoughts, and fly up near the ceiling (Space to rise).
"I flewed!" screamed Michael. Up and down they went, and round and round. "Heavenly" was Wendy's word.
"Come away!" Out of the window, into the night: second to the right, and straight on till morning.
Nana had broken her chain and fetched the parents, but too late. The birds were flown.
A speck of starlight from the second star
Second to the right, and straight on till morning
Fly through the ring of cloud ahead (Space to rise, C to sink).
How long they had been in the air they could not tell. Sometimes it was dark and sometimes light, and now they were very cold and again too warm.
On to the next ring of cloud.
Michael fell asleep, and dropped!
Michael has fallen asleep and dropped toward the sea. Dive and catch him!
Peter would wait till the last moment before he caught him; you were quicker. Michael never woke.
Back up, and on through the clouds.
They played follow-my-leader. Peter would fly off and come back laughing over something fearfully funny he had been saying to a star, which he had already forgotten.
Ask Peter how much further.
"Who are you?" he said, and then, "Wendy! I always forget." (You could not be sure he would remember you.) "Second to the right, and straight on till morning."
Straight on. Morning is coming.
"There it is," said Peter calmly. A million golden arrows were pointing out the island, all directed by their friend the sun.
The island! Through the last ring of cloud.
They knew it at once: it was the Neverland they had dreamed of. "John, there's the lagoon." "Wendy, look at the turtles burying their eggs."
Come down on the island.
The island came true. Then, all at once, it was afraid.
The Island Come True
The acorn button that stopped the arrow
Feeling that Peter was on his way back, the Neverland had again woke into life
Make your way to the Never Wood and the Hangman's Tree, where the Lost Boys live.

The Lost Boys were out looking for Peter, the pirates were out looking for the boys, the People of the Bluff were out looking for the pirates, and the beasts were out looking for the People of the Bluff. They were going round and round the island.
Meet the Lost Boys. Slightly is the most conceited.
"I'm Slightly. I remember the days before I was lost; I remember the manners and customs." (He did not.)
"The only thing I remember about my mother is that she often said to my father, 'Oh, how I wish I had a cheque-book of my own!'" None of them knew what a mother was, quite. They wished they had one.
Hide! Pirates are coming. Keep still among the toadstools.
"Avast, bully boys!" Hook sat down on a large mushroom... and jumped up again. It was hot. It was a chimney, and smoke came out. They had found the home under the ground.
listen (he does not see you)
Creep near and listen to Hook.

"We will leave a cake on the shore of the Mermaids' Lagoon, a large rich cake of a jolly thickness with green sugar on it. The boys have no mother to tell them how dangerous it is to eat rich damp cake."
Tick, tick, tick. Something is coming through the reeds. Keep still.
The crocodile! Hook ran for his life, Smee panting after. The crocodile had liked his hand so much that it followed him from sea to sea, licking its lips.
Tootles has his bow. Tinker Bell is tinkling at him.
"Peter wants you to shoot the Wendy." It was not in Tootles to question Peter's orders. "Out of the way, Tink!" He fired. Wendy fluttered to the ground with an arrow in her breast.
Something white is falling. Run to where it came down.
"This is no bird," said Tootles in a scared voice. "I think this must be a lady."
The arrow, caught on something
Look closely at the arrow.
The arrow had struck the acorn button, Peter's 'kiss', on its chain round her neck. "It is the kiss I gave her. It has saved her life." "She lives!"
A wisp of smoke from the top-hat chimney
Let us build a little house round her
Peter has come home. Hear what he says.
"I know," said Peter, "let us build a little house round her." They were all delighted. "Quick, bring me each of you the best of what we have. Gut our house. Be sharp."
A good straight branch
Another for the walls.
Gather branches for the walls of the little house.
In a moment they were as busy as tailors the night before a wedding. Clink, clink: the walls rose.
A soft cushion of moss
Moss for the roof.
Now moss and leaves for the roof.
"Let us make her a roof," and a fine green mossy roof it was.
Slightly says he will be the doctor. (He has borrowed John's hat.)
"Are you a doctor?" "Yes, my little man." He pretended to put a glass thing in her mouth. "She will do now. Give her beef tea out of a cup with a spout."
take it for the chimney
Every house needs a chimney. Find John's hat.
John's hat made a chimney, and at once smoke began to come out. Wendy, they say, was pleased.
Wendy wants roses peeping in at the window. Pick three.
"Oh, I wish I had a pretty house, the littlest ever seen, with funny little red walls, and roof of mossy green." Roses peeping in, and babies too (but they hadn't time for babies).
finish it round her
Finish the little house round her: walls, roof, chimney, door.
There it stood: red walls, a mossy green roof, John's hat smoking, and a door with a knocker made from the sole of Tootles's shoe.
Knock at the door. Wendy will open it.
"Where am I?" "Wendy lady, for you we built this house." "Oh, Wendy lady, be our mother." "Of course it's frightfully fascinating, but you see I am only a little girl." "That doesn't matter."
The Home Under the Ground
Down the hollow trees
Each of you is measured for your own hollow tree. Go down Peter's (E at the foot of the Hangman's Tree).
You go down as you would go down a chimney: draw in your breath, and down you go, at exactly the right speed.
A Never tree grows in the middle of the floor. Saw it off for a table.
